claim: Learning and memory storage is a complex process that has proven challenging to tackle.
source: Learning and memory storage is a complex process that has proven challenging to tackle.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: In nature, the instructive value of reinforcing experiences is likely acquired rather than innate.
source: It is likely that, in nature, the instructive value of reinforcing experiences is acquired rather than innate.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical position without specific experimental evidence in this manuscript.

claim: The association between seemingly neutral stimuli increases the gamut of possibilities to create meaningful associations and the predictive power of moment-by-moment experiences.
source: The association between seemingly neutral stimuli increases the gamut of possibilities to create meaningful associations and the predictive power of moment-by-moment experiences.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the function of associations.

claim: Flies show physiological evidence of olfactory unimodal sensory preconditioning.
source: Here, we report physiological and behavioral evidence of olfactory unimodal sensory preconditioning in fruit flies.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing depression to S2 odor in MBON neurons.

claim: The presentation of a pair of odors (S1 and S2) before one of them (S1) is associated with electric shocks elicits a conditional response not only to the trained odor (S1) but to the odor previously paired with it (S2).
source: We show that the presentation of a pair of odors (S1 and S2) before one of them (S1) is associated with electric shocks elicits a conditional response not only to the trained odor (S1) but to the odor previously paired with it (S2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral and physiological data presented in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The S2 odor elicits a conditional response even if it was never presented in contiguity with the aversive stimulus.
source: This occurs even if the S2 odor was never presented in contiguity with the aversive stimulus.
evidence: This is the defining characteristic of sensory preconditioning demonstrated in the experiments.

claim: Inhibition of the small G protein Rac1 facilitates the association between S1/S2 odors.
source: In addition, we show that inhibition of the small G protein Rac1, a known forgetting regulator, facilitates the association between S1/S2 odors.
evidence: Supported by data showing sensory preconditioning at longer ISIs in Rac1DN flies.

claim: Rac1 is a known forgetting regulator.
source: In addition, we show that inhibition of the small G protein Rac1, a known forgetting regulator, facilitates the association between S1/S2 odors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Rac1.

claim: Flies can infer value to olfactory stimuli based on the previous associative structure between odors.
source: These results indicate that flies can infer value to olfactory stimuli based on the previous associative structure between odors, and that inhibition of Rac1 lengthens the time window of the olfactory 'sensory buffer', allowing the establishment of associations between odors presented in sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sensory preconditioning results.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 lengthens the time window of the olfactory 'sensory buffer', allowing the establishment of associations between odors presented in sequence.
source: These results indicate that flies can infer value to olfactory stimuli based on the previous associative structure between odors, and that inhibition of Rac1 lengthens the time window of the olfactory 'sensory buffer', allowing the establishment of associations between odors presented in sequence.
evidence: Supported by data showing sensory preconditioning at 30s ISI in Rac1DN flies but not controls.

claim: A significant amount of what we know on the biological basis of learning and memory has come from studying classical conditioning.
source: A significant amount of what we know on the biological basis of learning and memory has come from studying classical conditioning, also known as Pavlovian conditioning (Heisenberg et al., 1985; Romanski et al., 1993; Uwano et al., 1995; LeDoux, 2000; Davis and Whalen, 2001; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Maren and Quirk, 2004; Fanselow and Poulos, 2005; Ehrlich et al., 2009; Johansen et al., 2010; Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Herry and Johansen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: During classical conditioning, learning depends on the contiguity of conditioned and unconditioned stimuli.
source: During classical conditioning, learning depends on the contiguity of conditioned and unconditioned stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about classical conditioning.

claim: In humans and other animals, the instructive value of naturally occurring reinforcing experiences is acquired rather than innately instructive and does not necessarily depend on mere contiguity.
source: Nevertheless, in humans and other animals, the instructive value of naturally occurring reinforcing experiences is acquired rather than innately instructive and does not necessarily dependent on mere contiguity.
evidence: This is a general statement about learning theory.

claim: The value of money and its capacity to function as a reinforcer is learned rather than innate.
source: For example, the value of money and its capacity to function as a reinforcer is learned rather than innate.
evidence: This is presented as an example of acquired reinforcement value.

claim: Learned behavioral control uses two types of information: habits/policies/cached values (model-free learning) and knowledge of the associative structure of the environment (model-based learning).
source: Learning theory has postulated the idea that learned behavioral control uses two types of information. The first results from habits, policies, or cached values (e.g., Pavlovian conditioning – model-free learning) (Jones et al., 2012). This kind of information produces a rapid, efficient behavioral response but does not consider changes in the value of the expected outcome. The second type of information relies on the knowledge of the associative structure of the environment to infer value (model-based learning).
evidence: This is supported by citation to learning theory literature.

claim: Model-free learning produces a rapid, efficient behavioral response but does not consider changes in the value of the expected outcome.
source: This kind of information produces a rapid, efficient behavioral response but does not consider changes in the value of the expected outcome.
evidence: This is a characteristic of model-free learning from learning theory.

claim: Acquiring new knowledge depends on creating an associative structure of external events, which is then used to create additional new meaningful associations.
source: In other words, acquiring new knowledge depends on creating an associative structure of external events, which is then used to create additional new meaningful associations (Daw et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2012; McDannald et al., 2012; Lucantonio et al., 2014; Sadacca et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to learning theory literature.

claim: In higher-order conditioning procedures, neutral stimuli acquire the property to elicit conditional responses even though they have never been in contiguity with a reinforcer.
source: In higher-order conditioning procedures, neutral stimuli acquire the property to elicit conditional responses even though they have never been in contiguity with a reinforcer.
evidence: This is a definition of higher-order conditioning.

claim: Sensory preconditioning is one example of higher-order conditioning.
source: Sensory preconditioning is one example of higher-order conditioning (Giurfa, 2013; Giurfa, 2015; Todd et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: In sensory preconditioning, two initially neutral stimuli (S1 and S2) are repeatedly presented in contiguity or in sequence (preconditioning phase); later, one of the stimuli (S1) is paired with a reinforcer (conditioning phase).
source: In sensory preconditioning, two initially neutral stimuli (S1 and S2) are repeatedly presented in contiguity or in sequence (preconditioning phase); later, one of the stimuli (S1) is paired with a reinforcer (conditioning phase).
evidence: This is a description of the sensory preconditioning procedure.

claim: After sensory preconditioning, S2 will elicit a conditioned response even though it was never paired with the reinforcer, indicating that the preconditioning phase created an association between S1 and S2.
source: After this, S2 will elicit a conditioned response even though it was never paired with the reinforcer, indicating that the preconditioning phase created an association between S1 and S2.
evidence: This describes the expected outcome of sensory preconditioning.

claim: The response to the preconditioned stimulus (S2) is not based on a mere association; instead, it must infer value by virtue of knowledge of the associative structure of the task.
source: The response to the preconditioned stimulus (S2) is different from the response to the reinforcer-paired S1 in that it is not based on a mere association; instead, it must infer value by virtue of knowledge of the associative structure of the task (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to learning theory.

claim: Sensory preconditioning has been shown previously in bees and flies.
source: Sensory preconditioning has been shown previously in bees and flies (Müller et al., 2000; Brembs and Heisenberg, 2001; Guo and Guo, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Guo and Guo (2005) trained flies using a flight simulator, using visual or olfactory cues to avoid certain flight directions.
source: Using a flight simulator (Guo and Guo, 2005), trained flies, using visual or olfactory cues to avoid certain flight directions.
evidence: This describes a prior study.

claim: Guo and Guo (2005) reported sensory preconditioning using S1–S2 cues of different modalities (olfactory and visual).
source: They reported sensory preconditioning using S1–S2 cues of different modalities (olfactory and visual).
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study.

claim: The Drosophila mushroom bodies (MB) are brain structures made up by the axons of the Kenyon cells (KC).
source: The Drosophila mushroom bodies (MB) are brain structures made up by the axons of the Kenyon cells (KC), and are known to play a central role in the encoding of olfactory memories (Heisenberg et al., 1985; Dubnau and Tully, 2001; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The mushroom bodies are known to play a central role in the encoding of olfactory memories.
source: The Drosophila mushroom bodies (MB) are brain structures made up by the axons of the Kenyon cells (KC), and are known to play a central role in the encoding of olfactory memories (Heisenberg et al., 1985; Dubnau and Tully, 2001; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During associative memory acquisition, positive or negative values are assigned to odors by associated reward and punishment, respectively.
source: During associative memory acquisition, positive or negative values are assigned to odors by associated reward and punishment, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about olfactory learning in Drosophila.

claim: Reinforcement is achieved by the coincident activation of a sparse number of KC by an odorant and the activation of dopaminergic neurons (DAN), which innervate the MB, by the unconditioned stimulus.
source: This reinforcement is achieved by the coincident activation of a sparse number of KC by an odorant and the activation of dopaminergic neurons (DAN), which innervate the MB, by the unconditioned stimulus.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of olfactory learning.

claim: Different DAN synapse onto discrete zones of the MB, resulting in 15 tile-like compartments of the MB.
source: Different DAN synapse onto discrete zones of the MB, resulting in 15 tile-like compartments of the MB.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the mushroom body.

claim: Each of the 15 tiled areas in the MB synapse onto the dendrites of distinct corresponding mushroom bodies output neurons (MBONs).
source: Each of these 15 tiled areas in turn synapse onto the dendrites of distinct corresponding mushroom bodies output neurons (MBONs).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Activation of different MBONs are known to alter behavioral approach or avoidance.
source: Activation of different MBONs are then known to alter behavioral approach or avoidance (Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Roselli et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The memory of an odor associated with an electric shock (classical conditioning) is known to be partially encoded as a decreased response specifically to the trained odor (CS+) in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β.
source: The memory of an odor associated with an electric shock (classical conditioning) is known to be partially encoded as a decreased response specifically to the trained odor (CS+) in a particular MBON known as MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Odors that have not been associated with an electric shock do not normally demonstrate decreased responses in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neuron.
source: Conversely, odors that have not been associated with an electric shock do not normally demonstrate decreased responses in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neuron (Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Flies expressing the dominant-negative form of Rac1N17 (Rac1DN) in adult KC displayed a depression to a non-shock associated odor in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neurons.
source: Thus, we were extremely surprised to report in a previous publication that flies expressing the dominant-negative form of Rac1N17 (Rac1DN) in adult KC using the temperature-dependent tool gal80ts (TARGET) (McGuire et al., 2003), displayed a depression to a non-shock associated odor in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neurons (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to a prior observation from the authors' previous work.

claim: Expressing Rac1N17 in KC significantly enhances trace conditioning, in which an odor is associated with an electric shock presented many seconds after odor offset.
source: It was also reported that expressing Rac1N17 in KC significantly enhances trace conditioning, in which an odor is associated with an electric shock presented many seconds after odor offset – suggesting that inhibition of Rac1 lengthens an olfactory 'sensory buffer' that later converges with the punishment signal (Shuai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 lengthens an olfactory 'sensory buffer' that later converges with the punishment signal.
source: It was also reported that expressing Rac1N17 in KC significantly enhances trace conditioning, in which an odor is associated with an electric shock presented many seconds after odor offset – suggesting that inhibition of Rac1 lengthens an olfactory 'sensory buffer' that later converges with the punishment signal (Shuai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation from a prior study.

claim: Control flies with a 1-s ISI during sensory preconditioning exhibit a decreased calcium response to the S2 odor in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neurons.
source: Interestingly however, when we shorten the sensory preconditioning interval to 1 s, the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neurons in control flies exhibit a decreased calcium response to the S2 odor, and to the S1 odor that is expected (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: With a 25- to 30-s ISI between preconditioned odors, there is no evidence of sensory preconditioning in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β of control animals.
source: Using the typical imaging protocol with a 25- to 30-s ISI between the preconditioned odors, we and others (Hige et al., 2015; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020) have shown there is no evidence of sensory preconditioning in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β of control animals.
evidence: Supported by current data and citations to prior work.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>α/β responses to naive odors remained unchanged during sensory preconditioning experiments, indicating the decrease in calcium response to the S2 odor is specific to the preconditioning phase.
source: Throughout these experiments, MBON-γ1pedc>α/β responses to naive odors remained unchanged, indicating the decrease in calcium response to the S2 odor is specific to the preconditioning phase, and not the result of a generalized depression to all odors (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1C showing no change in naive odor responses.

claim: Shortening the ISI window during sensory preconditioning allows control flies to form some association between the S1 and S2 odors.
source: This suggests that shortening the ISI window during sensory preconditioning allows control flies to form some association between the S1 and S2 odors, thus resulting in an inferred predictive value of the S2 odor after animals were aversively conditioned to the S1 odor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing depression to S2 at 1s ISI.

claim: Flies expressing dominant-negative Rac1N17 in the KC exhibit a decreased calcium response to the S2 odor when using an ISI of 30 s.
source: In contrast to control animals, flies expressing dominant-negative Rac1N17 in the KC had previously been found to exhibit a decreased calcium response to the S2 odor when using an ISI of 30 s (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When the ISI was increased to 5 min, no sensory preconditioning was observed in the Rac1DN animals.
source: When the ISI was increased to 5 min, no sensory preconditioning was observed in the Rac1DN animals (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies with the same genotype but raised at 18°C to prevent the expression of Rac1N17 showed the normal conditioning-induced odor depression to the S1 but no change to S2 with a preconditioning ISI window of 30 s.
source: This widening of the ISI window to allow for an S1/S2 association is dependent on the inhibition of Rac1, since flies with the same genotype but raised at 18°C to prevent the expression of Rac1N17 (using the TARGET system) showed the normal conditioning-induced odor depression to the S1 but no change to S2 with a preconditioning ISI window of 30 s (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Flies exposed to the same odor protocol except that the unconditioned stimulus was excluded showed no depression to either S1 or S2 odor.
source: We recorded olfactory responses in flies exposed to the same odor protocol except that the unconditioned stimulus was excluded. Results showed no depression to either S1 or S2 odor presented (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ratio between the mean of three initial responses and mean of three last responses in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β after 10 repeated presentations of both MCH and OCT was not significantly different between control and experimental genotypes.
source: Going even further, we confirmed this observation by recording and evaluating changes in calcium responses after 10 repeated presentations of both MCH and OCT. Data were analyzed as previously described (Hattori et al., 2017). The ratio between the mean of three initial responses and mean of three last responses in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β was not significantly different between control and experimental genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduced calcium response in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β to the classically conditioned S1 odor and the sensory preconditioned S2 odor cannot be explained by a general habituation to the odors due to the experimental protocol.
source: Thus, the reduced calcium response we see in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β to the classically conditioned S1 odor and the sensory preconditioned S2 odor cannot be explained by a general habituation to the odors due to the experimental protocol.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the habituation control experiments.

claim: Rac1 has been implicated in memory forgetting.
source: Rac1 has been implicated in memory forgetting, and it has been theorized that forgetting is fundamental for memory generalization (Richards and Frankland, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Forgetting is fundamental for memory generalization.
source: Rac1 has been implicated in memory forgetting, and it has been theorized that forgetting is fundamental for memory generalization (Richards and Frankland, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Hige et al. (2015) showed that a similar depression to the non-trained odor could result from a partial overlap in the neural representation of odors such as MCH and OCT.
source: In addition, (Hige et al., 2015) showed that a similar depression to the non-trained odor could result from a partial overlap in the neural representation of odors such as MCH and OCT.
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study.

claim: Similar sensory preconditioning results to MCH/OCT were obtained when using orthogonal odors PA and EL that are known to have little overlap in their KC representations.
source: For this, we trained animals using orthogonal odors, PA and EL, that are known to have little overlap in their KC representations. Surprisingly, similar results to MCH/OCT were obtained; we observed a depression to the non-trained S2 odor (EL) when Rac1 function is inhibited in KC (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The physiological response to sensory preconditioning can be observed for different odors and odor pairs.
source: Thus, this physiological response to sensory preconditioning can be observed for different odors and odor pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from multiple odor pairs.

claim: When the preconditioning association between the S1 and S2 odors was eliminated, results showed significant depression to the classically conditioned S1 odor but no depression to any other odors.
source: When we eliminated the preconditioning association between the S1 and S2 odors, the results showed significant depression to the classically conditioned S1 odor that was associated with the shock, but no depression to any other odors (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The depression to the non-trained S2 odor is dependent on the animal learning the association between S1 and S2 during the preconditioning stage.
source: These results demonstrate that the depression to the non-trained S2 odor was not due to a general depression to odors or generalization of learned aversion. Instead, depression of the non-trained S2 odor is dependent on the animal learning the association between S1 and S2 during the preconditioning stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control experiment without preconditioning.

claim: Control flies preconditioned with a single pairing of odors with a 1-s ISI did not demonstrate behavioral aversive memory to the S2 odor.
source: Despite observing evidence of sensory preconditioning by functional imaging using a similar protocol, we could not observe a behavioral memory to the non-shocked pre-paired odor (S2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Control flies preconditioned with 10 repeated presentations of odor pairings with an ISI of 1 s demonstrated a significant behavioral aversive memory expression to the S2 odor.
source: Thus, we preconditioned flies with 10 repeated presentations of odor pairings (S1/S2) before training (Figure 4A). Using an ISI of 1 s, this resulted in a significant behavioral aversive memory expression to the S2 odor in control flies (Figure 4B), consistent with our predictions based on the sensory preconditioning physiological data.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4B.

claim: Control flies did not demonstrate an aversive memory to the S2 odor when an ISI of 30 s was used with 10 repeated presentations.
source: Furthermore, control flies did not demonstrate an aversive memory to the S2 odor when an ISI of 30 s was used (Figure 4B), as would be predicted from our physiological imaging data.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4B.

claim: While a single odor pairing is sufficient to induce sensory preconditioned-related plasticity in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment, it is not enough for the S2 odor to drive the learned behavior.
source: These results also suggest that while a single odor pairing is sufficient to induce sensory preconditioned-related plasticity in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment, it is not enough for the S2 odor to drive the learned behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing physiological and behavioral results.

claim: The presentation of additional odor pairings recruits and induces sensory preconditioning-related plasticity in additional MB compartments, and it is the additive effect of multiple compartments that is necessary to drive the behavioral response.
source: We suggest that the presentation of additional odor pairings recruits and induces sensory preconditioning-related plasticity in additional MB compartments, and it is the additive effect of multiple compartments that is necessary to drive the behavioral response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: A short pairing of odor and shock (1-s odor paired with 4 DAN photostimulation pulses) is enough to induce plasticity in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment but not in MBON-α2sc.
source: Similar phenomena have been observed before for classical conditioning where a short pairing of odor and shock – 1-s odor paired with 4 DAN photostimulation pulses – is enough to induce plasticity in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment but not in MBON-α2sc.
evidence: This refers to prior observations.

claim: Longer training protocols (1-min odor presentation paired with 120 DAN photostimulation pulses) induce plasticity in MBON-α2sc.
source: Longer training protocols – 1-min odor presentation paired with 120 DAN photostimulation pulses – induce plasticity in MBON-α2sc (Hige et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Preconditioning flies with MCH/OCT pairs repeated 10 times before training resulted in a robust depression in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β to the non-shocked pre-paired odor (CS2) in control flies.
source: Physiologically, preconditioning flies with MCH/OCT pairs repeated 10 times before training resulted in a robust depression in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β to the non-shocked pre-paired odor (CS2) in control flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Similar physiological results were obtained when PA/EL were used as the preconditioned odors with 10 repeated presentations.
source: These results were similar when PA/EL were used as the preconditioned odors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A 30-s ISI resulted in no aversive memory to S2 in control flies, but a significant aversive memory was observed in flies expressing Rac1N17.
source: As would be predicted from our physiological data, while a 30-s ISI resulted in no aversive memory to S2 in control flies, a significant aversive memory was observed in flies expressing Rac1N17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4B.

claim: Lengthening the ISI to 5 min eliminated behavioral sensory preconditioning both in controls and in flies expressing Rac1N17.
source: Further lengthening the ISI to 5 min eliminated behavioral sensory preconditioning both in controls and in flies expressing Rac1N17 (Figure 4B), again mirroring the physiological results in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β neuron (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4B.

claim: Flies kept at 18°C to prevent expression of Rac1N17 behaved as control flies and did not demonstrate behavioral evidence of sensory preconditioning when using an ISI of 30 min.
source: Flies kept at 18°C to prevent expression of Rac1N17 behaved as control flies and did not demonstrate behavioral evidence of sensory preconditioning when using an ISI of 30 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rac1N17 expression in KC did not alter olfactory responses in the MB lobes, even when recordings were performed at a higher speed (28 Hz).
source: Finally, we tested if Rac1N17 expression in KC altered olfactory responses in the MB lobes. Interestingly, we could not find any change in the calcium response dynamics in KC γ lobes, even when recordings were performed at a higher speed (28 Hz) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Memories are not discrete bits of events and associations that are added and accumulated in our brains.
source: Memories are not discrete bits of events and associations that are added and accumulated in our brains.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of memory.

claim: Memories are dynamic; they undergo modifications and updates and are integrated into a coherent story that continuously incorporates new information to predict upcoming events better and to inform decision making.
source: Rather, memories are dynamic; they undergo modifications and updates and are integrated into a coherent story that continuously incorporates new information to predict upcoming events better and to inform decision making.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about memory function.

claim: Within the complex associative structure of memories, associations between seemingly valueless stimuli are fundamental.
source: Within this complex associative structure, associations between seemingly valueless stimuli are fundamental.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by the sensory preconditioning findings.

claim: Even the simple brain of a fly can form associations between seemingly valueless stimuli.
source: Here we present evidence that even the simple brain of a fly can form these associations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sensory preconditioning data.

claim: DAN are essential for many types of reinforcement and even for non-associative learning like novelty detection.
source: We know that DAN are essential for many types of reinforcement and even for non-associative learning like novelty detection (Hattori et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Dopamine neurons receive substantial feedback from both KC and MBON.
source: Furthermore, we know dopamine neurons receive substantial feedback from both KC and MBON.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: While a single odor pairing is sufficient to induce sensory preconditioned-related plasticity in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment, it is not enough for the S2 odor to drive the learned behavior.
source: Another interesting finding is that while a single odor pairing is sufficient to induce sensory preconditioned-related plasticity in the MBON-γ1pedc>α/β compartment, it is not enough for the S2 odor to drive the learned behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing physiological and behavioral data.

claim: There is accumulating evidence that memorable experiences are encoded in parallel, relatively independent memory traces, and it is the integration of these different memory traces that drives the most adequate behavior.
source: There is accumulating evidence that memorable experiences are encoded in parallel, relatively independent memory traces, and it is the integration of these different memory traces that drives the most adequate behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about memory systems.

claim: Examples of parallel memory traces include the additive effect of aversive memory traces.
source: Examples include the additive effect of aversive memory traces (Aso et al., 2012); the additive effect of contextual memory to aversive olfactory memories (Zhao et al., 2019); or the integration of parallel opposite memories during memory extinction (Felsenberg et al., 2017; Felsenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Calcium is a good proxy of neuronal activity within the KC.
source: While calcium is a good proxy of neuronal activity within the KC, it does not necessarily directly translate to a readout of the neurotransmission output of the KC and its communication with downstream neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of calcium imaging.

claim: Calcium does not necessarily directly translate to a readout of the neurotransmission output of the KC and its communication with downstream neurons.
source: While calcium is a good proxy of neuronal activity within the KC, it does not necessarily directly translate to a readout of the neurotransmission output of the KC and its communication with downstream neurons.
evidence: This is a caveat about interpreting calcium imaging data.

claim: Inhibiting Rac1 in KC during development results in lethality.
source: The Target system was used because inhibiting Rac1 in KC during development results in lethality.
evidence: This explains the experimental design choice.

claim: S1 (MCH) responses were completely depressed 5 min after training in control flies preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI.
source: S1 (MCH) responses were completely depressed 5 min after training in control flies preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI. Non-parametric Mann–Whitney test p ≤ 0.0044; n = 8–10.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1C.

claim: A significant inhibition of post-trained response to S2 (OCT) was observed in control flies preconditioned with 1-s ISI.
source: A significant inhibition of post-trained response to S2 (OCT) was observed in control flies preconditioned with 1-s ISI. Non-parametric Mann–Whitney test p = 0.035; n = 10.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1C.

claim: S2 (OCT) responses in control flies preconditioned with 30-s or 5-min ISI showed no significant change.
source: In contrast, S2 (OCT) responses in control flies preconditioned with 30-s or 5-min ISI showed no significant change. Non-parametric Mann–Whitney test p ≥ 0.0630, n = 8–10.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1C.

claim: Neither naive odor (PA and EL) responses showed any significant reduction in control flies preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI.
source: Neither naive odor (penthyl acetate [PA] and ethyl lactate [EL]) responses showed any significant reduction in flies preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI. Non-parametric Mann–Whitney test p ≥ 0.0726, n = 8–10.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1C.

claim: S1 (MCH) responses were completely depressed 5 min after training in flies expressing Rac1N17 preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI.
source: S1 (MCH) responses were completely depressed 5 min after training in flies expressing Rac1N17 preconditioned with 1-s, 30-s, or 5-min ISI. Non-parametric Mann–Whitney test p ≤ 0.0009; n = 8–12.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 1D.
